claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3K–M.

claims.claim: TIAM-1/GEF functions downstream of or in parallel to DMA-1/LRR-TM (and possibly hpo-30/Claudin) and in a manner that depends on ACT-4/Actin.
claims.source: Taken together, our experiments suggest a pathway, in which TIAM-1/GEF functions downstream of or in parallel to DMA-1/LRR-TM (and possibly hpo-30/Claudin) and in a manner that depends on ACT-4/Actin.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from genetic epistasis experiments.

claims.claim: Both DMA-1/LRR-TM and HPO-30/Claudin are predicted transmembrane proteins functioning in PVD dendrites.
claims.source: Both DMA-1/LRR-TM and HPO-30/Claudin are predicted transmembrane proteins functioning in PVD dendrites.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about protein structure and function.

claims.claim: The DMA::GFP reporter is localized in a punctate fashion in the cell body and along the dendritic tree as well as on the membrane, visible as diffuse membrane staining throughout the whole dendritic tree.
claims.source: As previously reported (Dong et al., 2016), the DMA::GFP reporter is localized in a punctate fashion in the cell body and along the dendritic tree as well as on the membrane, visible as diffuse membrane staining throughout the whole dendritic tree (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature and data shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: An HPO-30::tagBFP fusion exhibited localized punctate and diffuse membrane staining along the dendritic processes with less staining in the axon of PVD neurons.
claims.source: We found that an HPO-30::tagBFP fusion also exhibited localized punctate and diffuse membrane staining along the dendritic processes with less staining in the axon of PVD neurons (Figure 4A), much like other recently described HPO-30::GFP reporters (Smith et al., 2013; Zou et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4A and citations to published literature.

claims.claim: The DMA-1::GFP and HPO-30::tagBFP puncta show significant but not complete colocalization in dendritic processes.
claims.source: The DMA-1::GFP and HPO-30:: tagBFP puncta show significant but not complete colocalization in dendritic processes, suggesting that at least some fraction of these proteins are closely associated (Figure 4C–D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4C–D.

claims.claim: DMA-1.HA efficiently co-precipitated HPO-30.V5 from a cellular lysate.
claims.source: We found that DMA-1.HA efficiently co-precipitated HPO-30.V5 from a cellular lysate, suggesting that both proteins are part of the same biochemical complex (Figure 4F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4F.

claims.claim: DMA-1 and HPO-30 are part of the same biochemical complex.
claims.source: We found that DMA-1.HA efficiently co-precipitated HPO-30.V5 from a cellular lysate, suggesting that both proteins are part of the same biochemical complex (Figure 4F).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from co-immunoprecipitation data.

claims.claim: The biochemical interaction between DMA-1 and HPO-30 was independent of the intracellular domain of DMA-1.
claims.source: This biochemical interaction was independent of the intracellular domain of DMA-1 (Figure 4G), suggesting that the proteins interact through either the transmembrane segments or the extracellular domains of DMA-1.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4G.

claims.claim: DMA-1 and HPO-30 interact through either the transmembrane segments or the extracellular domains of DMA-1.
claims.source: This biochemical interaction was independent of the intracellular domain of DMA-1 (Figure 4G), suggesting that the proteins interact through either the transmembrane segments or the extracellular domains of DMA-1.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from co-immunoprecipitation data.

claims.claim: Overexpression of the HPO-30::tagBFP reporter in PVD resulted in significantly reduced fluorescent intensity of the DMA-1::GFP reporter in 1° dendrites compared to control animals.
claims.source: We noticed that overexpression of the HPO-30::tagBFP reporter in PVD resulted in significantly reduced fluorescent intensity of the DMA-1::GFP reporter in 1° dendrites compared to control animals (Figure 4H,I).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4H,I.

claims.claim: Loss of hpo-30/Claudin resulted in an increase of diffuse dendrite staining of the DMA-1::GFP reporter in 3° but not in 1° dendrites.
claims.source: Conversely, loss of hpo-30/Claudin resulted in an increase of diffuse dendrite staining of the DMA-1::GFP reporter in 3° but not in 1° dendrites (Figure J-L).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4J-L.

claims.claim: The number of DMA-1::GFP puncta in 1° and 3° branches was reduced in hpo-30 null mutants, although their relative distribution remained unchanged.
claims.source: In addition, we found the number of DMA-1::GFP puncta in 1° and 3° branches reduced in hpo-30 null mutants, although their relative distribution remained unchanged (Figure 4M–O).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4M–O.

claims.claim: The diffuse staining of DMA-1::GFP represents the surface membrane fraction while punctate staining represents the vesicular fraction.
claims.source: It has been suggested that the diffuse staining of DMA-1::GFP represents the surface membrane fraction while punctate staining represents the vesicular fraction (Taylor et al., 2015; Zou et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claims.claim: The normal function of HPO-30/Claudin is to negatively regulate the DMA-1/LRR-TM surface membrane fraction and to increase the vesicular fraction.
claims.source: Therefore, our results suggest that the normal function of HPO-30/Claudin is to negatively regulate the DMA-1/LRR-TM surface membrane fraction and to increase the vesicular fraction.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from imaging experiments.

claims.claim: In both wild type and hpo-30 mutant animals, DMA-1::GFP puncta fell into a mobile and a stationary fraction.
claims.source: We found that in both genotypes, DMA-1::GFP puncta fell into a mobile and a stationary fraction, respectively.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by time lapse imaging data.

claims.claim: The mobile fraction of DMA-1::GFP exhibited a wide range of moving speeds in both retrograde and anterograde directions.
claims.source: The mobile fraction exhibited a wide range of moving speeds in both retrograde and anterograde directions.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by time lapse imaging data.

claims.claim: The number of mobile DMA-1::GFP puncta was decreased in hpo-30 mutant animals compared to wild type animals, while the number of immobile DMA-1::GFP puncta remained unchanged.
claims.source: Intriguingly, the number of mobile DMA-1::GFP puncta was decreased in hpo-30 mutant animals compared to wild type animals, while the number of immobile DMA-1::GFP puncta remained unchanged (Figure 4R).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4R.

claims.claim: HPO-30/Claudin exists in a complex with DMA-1/LRR-TM.
claims.source: Collectively, we conclude that (1) HPO-30/Claudin exists in a complex with DMA-1/LRR-TM, that (2) HPO-30 negatively regulates DMA-1::GFP membrane levels and, that (3) HPO-30 serves a function in trafficking of DMA-1::GFP vesicles.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from co-immunoprecipitation and imaging data.

claims.claim: HPO-30 negatively regulates DMA-1::GFP membrane levels.
claims.source: Collectively, we conclude that (1) HPO-30/Claudin exists in a complex with DMA-1/LRR-TM, that (2) HPO-30 negatively regulates DMA-1::GFP membrane levels and, that (3) HPO-30 serves a function in trafficking of DMA-1::GFP vesicles.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from imaging data.

claims.claim: HPO-30 serves a function in trafficking of DMA-1::GFP vesicles.
claims.source: Collectively, we conclude that (1) HPO-30/Claudin exists in a complex with DMA-1/LRR-TM, that (2) HPO-30 negatively regulates DMA-1::GFP membrane levels and, that (3) HPO-30 serves a function in trafficking of DMA-1::GFP vesicles.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from time lapse imaging data.

claims.claim: C. elegans TIAM-1/GEF is a multidomain protein which comprises, in order, a myristoylation signal, an EVH1 (Ena/Vasp homology) domain, a PDZ domain, and a DH/PH (Dbl homology domain/plekstrin homology domain) encoding the enzymatic guanine nucleotide exchange activity.
claims.source: C. elegans TIAM-1/GEF is a multidomain protein (Figure 5A), which comprises, in order, a myristoylation signal, an EVH1 (Ena/Vasp homology) domain, a PDZ domain, and a DH/PH (Dbl homology domain/plekstrin homology domain) encoding the enzymatic guanine nucleotide exchange activity (Demarco et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature and schematic shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: C. elegans TIAM-1/GEF can shape neurons through mechanisms dependent on the small GTPases mig-2/RhoG and ced-10/Rac1.
claims.source: Consistent with work in flies and vertebrate neurons (Sone et al., 1997; Kunda et al., 2001; Tolias et al., 2005), C. elegans TIAM-1/GEF can shape neurons through mechanisms dependent on the small GTPases mig-2/RhoG and ced-10/Rac1 (Demarco et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claims.claim: Neither mutations in mig-2/RhoG and ced-10/Rac1 alone or in combination, nor a mutation in rac-2 resulted in obvious phenotypes in PVD dendritic arbor formation.
claims.source: Surprisingly, neither mutations in mig-2/RhoG and ced-10/Rac1 alone or in combination, nor a mutation in rac-2 resulted in obvious phenotypes in PVD dendritic arbor formation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–C), implying that TIAM-1/GEF could function independently of these Rac1-like GTPases, at least individually.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–C.

claims.claim: TIAM-1/GEF could function independently of Rac1-like GTPases, at least individually.
claims.source: Surprisingly, neither mutations in mig-2/RhoG and ced-10/Rac1 alone or in combination, nor a mutation in rac-2 resulted in obvious phenotypes in PVD dendritic arbor formation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–C), implying that TIAM-1/GEF could function independently of these Rac1-like GTPases, at least individually.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from genetic analysis.

claims.claim: Full length TIAM-1/GEF alone or as a C-terminal fusion with mCherry fully rescued the PVD dendrite patterning defects.
claims.source: We found that full length TIAM-1/GEF alone or as a C-terminal fusion with mCherry fully rescued the PVD dendrite patterning defects (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: A T548F point mutant of full length TIAM-1/GEF still rescued the PVD mutant phenotype.
claims.source: Surprisingly, a T548F point mutant of full length TIAM-1/GEF still rescued the PVD mutant phenotype (Figure 6B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: The T548F mutation in the C. elegans TIAM-1 DH/PH domain abolishes Rac1 GEF activity in vitro.
claims.source: The fact that the very same mutation in the C. elegans TIAM-1 DH/PH domain (Demarco et al., 2012) as well as the analogous point mutation in the UNC-73/Trio GEF abolishes Rac1 GEF activity in vitro (Steven et al., 1998), lent further support to the idea that TIAM-1/GEF activity may not be required for PVD patterning (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claims.claim: Two independently isolated alleles (dz264 and dz265) that harbored the T548F point mutation in the tiam-1/GEF locus appeared phenotypically normal in regard to PVD patterning.
claims.source: Two independently isolated alleles (dz264 and dz265) that harbored the T548F point mutation in the tiam-1/GEF locus appeared phenotypically normal in regard to PVD patterning (Figure 6C–D and data not shown).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6C–D.

claims.claim: A point mutant form of TIAM-1 (T548F) devoid of measurable Rac1 GEF activity in vitro is sufficient for PVD patterning in vivo.
claims.source: Thus, a point mutant form of TIAM-1 (T548F) devoid of measurable Rac1 GEF activity in vitro is sufficient for PVD patterning in vivo.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from rescue experiments with TIAM-1(T548F).

claims.claim: TIAM-1/GEF can function independently of its GEF enzymatic activity.
claims.source: In summary, our results suggest that TIAM-1/GEF can function independently of its GEF enzymatic activity although we can not formally exclude that the TIAM-1(T548F) shows enzymatic activity towards small GTPases other than Rac1 that may be involved in PVD patterning.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from rescue experiments, with a caveat about possible activity toward other GTPases.

claims.claim: Removing the PDZ ligand motif of DMA-1/LRR-TM results in a decrease in 4° branches but not 2° or 3° branches.
claims.source: First, removing the PDZ ligand motif of DMA-1/LRR-TM results in a decrease in 4° branches but not 2° or 3° branches.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data from experiments with dma-1(ΔPDZ) mutants.

claims.claim: A GEF-only construct of TIAM-1/GEF, which lacks the PDZ domain, rescues the 3° branching defects, but not 4° branching defects of tiam-1 mutant animals.
claims.source: Conversely, a GEF-only construct of TIAM-1/GEF, which lacks the PDZ domain, rescues the 3° branching defects, but not 4° branching defects of tiam-1 mutant animals.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data from transgenic rescue experiments.

claims.claim: Compromising the PDZ-mediated interaction between TIAM-1/GEF and DMA-1/LRR-TM results in specific loss of 4° branching.
claims.source: Thus, compromising the PDZ-mediated interaction between TIAM-1/GEF and DMA-1/LRR-TM results in specific loss of 4° branching.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from genetic and rescue experiments.

claims.claim: TIAM-1/GEF interacts with DMA-1/LRR-TM through the PDZ motif at the C-terminus of DMA-1 and the PDZ-binding domain of TIAM-1.
claims.source: Furthermore, immunoprecipitation assays strongly indicate that TIAM-1/GEF and DMA-1/LRR-TM can interact directly through the PDZ motif at the C-terminus of DMA-1 and the PDZ-binding domain of TIAM-1.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data.

claims.claim: tiam-1 overexpression resulted in excessive branching.
claims.source: Since tiam-1 overexpression resulted in excessive branching, TIAM-1/GEF may promote branching in a dose-dependent manner.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data from overexpression experiments.

claims.claim: TIAM-1/GEF may promote branching in a dose-dependent manner.
claims.source: Since tiam-1 overexpression resulted in excessive branching, TIAM-1/GEF may promote branching in a dose-dependent manner.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from overexpression experiments.

claims.claim: The PDZ interaction with DMA-1 recruits TIAM-1/GEF to specific subcellular locations, where a locally higher concentration of TIAM-1/GEF induces dendrite branching.
claims.source: We propose that the PDZ interaction with DMA-1 recruits TIAM-1/GEF to specific subcellular locations, where a locally higher concentration of TIAM-1/GEF induces dendrite branching.
claims.evidence: The claim is a proposed model based on inference from multiple experiments.

claims.claim: A TIAM-1::GFP reporter expressed in PVD is recruited to higher order dendritic branches by DMA-1/LRR-TM.
claims.source: These findings are also consistent with a recent study, which also suggested that a TIAM-1::GFP reporter expressed in PVD is recruited to higher order dendritic branches by DMA-1/LRR-TM (Zou et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claims.claim: The PDZ-mediated interaction of TIAM-1/GEF and DMA-1/LRR-TM interaction is required for normal 4° dendrite formation.
claims.source: Collectively, these findings suggest that the PDZ-mediated interaction of TIAM-1/GEF and DMA-1/LRR-TM interaction is required for normal 4° dendrite formation.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from multiple experiments.

claims.claim: Transgenic expression of a TIAM-1(GEF-only) construct lacking the PDZ interaction domain can rescue both the formation of 2° and 3° PVD branches.
claims.source: An intriguing finding is that transgenic expression of a TIAM-1(GEF-only) construct lacking the PDZ interaction domain can rescue both the formation of 2° and 3° PVD branches.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data from transgenic rescue experiments.

claims.claim: DMA-1/LRR-TM lacking the cytoplasmic domain was still capable of rescuing 2° and 3° branching number (but not extension).
claims.source: Conversely, DMA-1/LRR-TM lacking the cytoplasmic domain was still capable of rescuing 2° and 3° branching number (but not extension), suggesting that protein interactions of the DMA-1 transmembrane or the extracellular domain, possibly in conjunction with TIAM-1/GEF may mediate an alternative parallel pathway.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data from transgenic rescue experiments.

claims.claim: Protein interactions of the DMA-1 transmembrane or the extracellular domain, possibly in conjunction with TIAM-1/GEF may mediate an alternative parallel pathway.
claims.source: Conversely, DMA-1/LRR-TM lacking the cytoplasmic domain was still capable of rescuing 2° and 3° branching number (but not extension), suggesting that protein interactions of the DMA-1 transmembrane or the extracellular domain, possibly in conjunction with TIAM-1/GEF may mediate an alternative parallel pathway.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from rescue experiments.

claims.claim: DMA-1/LRR-TM colocalizes with the HPO-30/Claudin.
claims.source: Indeed, imaging experiments and biochemical assays suggest that (1) DMA-1/LRR-TM colocalizes with the HPO-30/Claudin and that (2) both proteins can form a biochemical complex through an interaction independent of the cytoplasmic domain of DMA-1.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by imaging and biochemical data.

claims.claim: DMA-1 and HPO-30 can form a biochemical complex through an interaction independent of the cytoplasmic domain of DMA-1.
claims.source: Indeed, imaging experiments and biochemical assays suggest that (1) DMA-1/LRR-TM colocalizes with the HPO-30/Claudin and that (2) both proteins can form a biochemical complex through an interaction independent of the cytoplasmic domain of DMA-1.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by biochemical data.

claims.claim: hpo-30 double mutants with tiam-1 or sax-7/L1CAM display enhanced phenotypes consistent with functions in parallel pathways.
claims.source: Moreover, genetic double mutant analyses show that hpo-30 double mutants with tiam-1 or sax-7/L1CAM display enhanced phenotypes consistent with functions in parallel pathways.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by genetic epistasis analysis.

claims.claim: Mutating components of the WASP family verprolin-homologous protein (WVE-1/WAVE) regulatory complex (WRC) of actin regulators result in defects in PVD patterning.
claims.source: Previous studies have shown that mutating components of the WASP family verprolin-homologous protein (WVE-1/WAVE) regulatory complex (WRC) of actin regulators result in defects in PVD patterning (Aguirre-Chen et al., 2011; Zou et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claims.claim: HPO-30 can physically interact with the WRC.
claims.source: Moreover, HPO-30 can physically interact with the WRC and, compromising the molecular interactions between both DMA-1 and TIAM-1 and, between HPO-30 and the WRC at the same time result in synergistic defects consistent with the notion of parallel pathways downstream of the DMA-1 receptor (Zou et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claims.claim: Compromising the molecular interactions between both DMA-1 and TIAM-1 and, between HPO-30 and the WRC at the same time result in synergistic defects consistent with the notion of parallel pathways downstream of the DMA-1 receptor.
claims.source: Moreover, HPO-30 can physically interact with the WRC and, compromising the molecular interactions between both DMA-1 and TIAM-1 and, between HPO-30 and the WRC at the same time result in synergistic defects consistent with the notion of parallel pathways downstream of the DMA-1 receptor (Zou et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claims.claim: The DMA-1/LRR-TM receptor, in conjunction with HPO-30/Claudin and TIAM-1/GEF recruit actin regulators to the membrane to form dendritic branches.
claims.source: Zou et al. proposed that the DMA-1/LRR-TM receptor, in conjunction with HPO-30/Claudin and TIAM-1/GEF recruit actin regulators to the membrane to form dendritic branches.
claims.evidence: The claim is a model proposed by another study.

claims.claim: Recruitment of the WRC by HPO-30 may serve a role in endocytosis of DMA-1::GFP, as the WRC is known to play a role in clathrin-mediated endocytosis.
claims.source: Alternatively, and consistent with our observation that HPO-30 negatively regulates the surface localization of the DMA-1/LRR-TM reporter, recruitment of the WRC by HPO-30 may also serve a role in endocytosis of DMA-1::GFP, as the WRC is known to play a role in clathrin-mediated endocytosis (Mooren et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: The claim is a speculative alternative model based on inference and citation to published literature.

claims.claim: The act-4(dz222) allele results in more distal localization of DMA-1::GFP, including at the tip of growing dendrites.
claims.source: In possible support of such a function, the act-4(dz222) allele results in more distal localization of DMA-1::GFP, including at the tip of growing dendrites (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D,E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D,E.

claims.claim: Depolymerizing F-actin in vivo results in severe defects in PVD patterning.
claims.source: First, depolymerizing F-actin in vivo results in severe defects in PVD patterning (Harterink et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claims.claim: F-actin is localized to the distal tips of developing PVD dendrites and appears mutually exclusive with microtubules.
claims.source: Second, F-actin is localized to the distal tips of developing PVD dendrites and appears mutually exclusive with microtubules.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 7.

claims.claim: F-actin localization to distal dendrites depends on the presence of transmembrane receptors on PVD dendrites and their ligands.
claims.source: Third, we find that F-actin localization to distal dendrites depends on the presence of transmembrane receptors on PVD dendrites and their ligands.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data in mutants shown in Figure 7.

claims.claim: RNAi-mediated gene knock down of other genes with possible or established roles as regulators of F-actin in developing axons such as unc-44/Ankyrin, unc-115/Ablim, or unc-70/β-spectrin, display similar defects in PVD dendrite patterning as act-4/Actin and tiam-1/GEF mutants.
claims.source: Lastly, RNAi-mediated gene knock down of other genes with possible or established roles as regulators of F-actin in developing axons such as unc-44/Ankyrin (Otsuka et al., 1995), unc-115/Ablim (Lundquist et al., 1998; Struckhoff and Lundquist, 2003), or unc-70/β-spectrin (Hammarlund et al., 2000), display similar defects in PVD dendrite patterning as act-4/Actin and tiam-1/GEF mutants (Aguirre-Chen et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claims.claim: The DMA-1/LRR-TM receptor is part of a biochemical complex with the TIAM-1/GEF and ACT-4/Actin.
claims.source: Our experiments show that the DMA-1/LRR-TM receptor is part of a biochemical complex with the TIAM-1/GEF and ACT-4/Actin.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 7.

claims.claim: Binding of the DMA-1/LRR-TM receptor by the extracellular SAX-7/MNR-1/LECT-2 ligand complex could result in recruitment of TIAM-1/GEF, ACT-4/Actin and DMA-1/LRR-TM in a complex, thereby directly linking the receptor to the cytoskeleton.
claims.source: In analogy, binding of the DMA-1/LRR-TM receptor by the extracellular SAX-7/MNR-1/LECT-2 ligand complex could result in recruitment of TIAM-1/GEF, ACT-4/Actin and DMA-1/LRR-TM in a complex, thereby directly linking the receptor to the cytoskeleton.
claims.evidence: The claim is a proposed model based on inference from biochemical and genetic data.

claims.claim: The interaction between TIAM-1/GEF and ACT-4/Actin is likely specific.
claims.source: The interaction between TIAM-1/GEF and ACT-4/Actin is likely specific, because animals carrying the act-4(dz222) missense allele are viable without other obvious phenotypes.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from phenotypic analysis.

claims.claim: The exact same molecular change in act-4 (G151E) was identified by Zou et al. (2018) in their screen for genes involved in PVD patterning.
claims.source: In support of the specificity of the dz222 allele, it is worth noting that the exact same molecular change was identified by Zou et al. (2018) in their screen for genes involved in PVD patterning.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claims.claim: The phenotype of act-4(dz222) is in stark contrast to the embryonic lethality observed upon continuous RNAi-mediated knockdown of act-4.
claims.source: The phenotype of act-4(dz222) is in stark contrast to the embryonic lethality observed upon continuous RNAi-mediated knockdown of act-4 (Gottschalk et al., 2005, data not shown).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature and unpublished data.

claims.claim: Knock down of ACT-4/Actin by RNAi during larval stages and the G151E missense mutation in ACT-4/Actin encoded by the act-4(dz222) allele result in similar phenotypes in PVD dendrites.
claims.source: Moreover, knock down of ACT-4/Actin by RNAi during larval stages on the one hand and, the G151E missense mutation in ACT-4/Actin encoded by the act-4(dz222) allele on the other hand result in similar phenotypes in PVD dendrites.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of RNAi and mutant phenotypes.

claims.claim: Loss of ACT-4 is as detrimental for dendrite patterning as the stronger biochemical interaction between TIAM-1 and ACT-4(G151E).
claims.source: In other words, loss of ACT-4 is as detrimental for dendrite patterning as the stronger biochemical interaction between TIAM-1 and ACT-4(G151E).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from phenotypic and biochemical data.

claims.claim: The interaction between TIAM-1 and ACT-4, and possibly DMA-1/LRR-TM has to be transient or dynamic.
claims.source: This suggests that the interaction between TIAM-1 and ACT-4, and possibly DMA-1/LRR-TM has to be transient or dynamic.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from phenotypic and biochemical data.

claims.claim: The strong interaction between ACT-4(G151E) and TIAM-1/GEF could sequester actin from the polymerizing pool.
claims.source: Alternatively, the strong interaction between ACT-4(G151E) and TIAM-1/GEF could sequester actin from the polymerizing pool.
claims.evidence: The claim is a speculative alternative explanation.

claims.claim: A point mutation in β-spectrin, which increases the affinity of β-spectrin with actin one thousand fold, results in defects in Drosophila dendrite arborization neuron.
claims.source: These findings are reminiscent of a point mutation in β-spectrin, which by increasing the affinity of β-spectrin with actin one thousand fold, results in defects in Drosophila dendrite arborization neuron (Avery et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claims.claim: At least two partially redundant pathways act downstream of the DMA-1/LRR-TM receptor.
claims.source: Collectively, our studies and the findings by Zou et al. (Zou et al., 2018) suggest that at least two partially redundant pathways act downstream of the DMA-1/LRR-TM receptor.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from multiple experiments in this study and cited literature.

claims.claim: In one pathway, DMA-1 interacts via HPO-30/Claudin with the WRC during patterning of lower order branches.
claims.source: In one pathway, DMA-1 interacts via HPO-30/Claudin with the WRC during patterning of lower order branches, whereas the interaction with TIAM-1/GEF may directly link the receptor complex with the actin cytoskeleton during 4° dendrite formation.
claims.evidence: The claim is a proposed model based on inference from multiple experiments.

claims.claim: The interaction with TIAM-1/GEF may directly link the receptor complex with the actin cytoskeleton during 4° dendrite formation.
claims.source: In one pathway, DMA-1 interacts via HPO-30/Claudin with the WRC during patterning of lower order branches, whereas the interaction with TIAM-1/GEF may directly link the receptor complex with the actin cytoskeleton during 4° dendrite formation.
claims.evidence: The claim is a proposed model based on inference from multiple experiments.

claims.claim: Tiam1 in vertebrates has been shown to serve important functions during nervous system patterning.
claims.source: Tiam1 in vertebrates has been shown to serve important functions during nervous system patterning (Yoo et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claims.claim: Knock down and overexpression experiments established functions for Tiam1 in axon growth cone formation and, activity-dependent remodeling of dendritic arbors in vitro and in vivo.
claims.source: Knock down and overexpression experiments further established functions for Tiam1 in axon growth cone formation and, activity-dependent remodeling of dendritic arbors in vitro and in vivo (Kunda et al., 2001; Tolias et al., 2005; Tolias et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

results.result: The dendritic arbors of PVD neurons in C. elegans are patterned by distinct pathways downstream of the DMA-1/LRR-TM receptor. DMA-1 interacts through a PDZ ligand motif with TIAM-1/GEF in a complex with ACT-4/Actin to pattern 4° dendrite branches by localizing F-actin to distal ends of developing dendrites. TIAM-1/GEF functions independently of Rac1 GEF activity. A partially redundant pathway dependent on HPO-30/Claudin regulates formation of 2° and 3° branches, possibly by regulating membrane localization and trafficking of DMA-1/LRR-TM.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C6 represent the core findings of the manuscript and are well-supported by multiple lines of evidence including genetic screens (C19-C23), epistasis analysis (C41-C49), rescue experiments (C34-C40, C85-C89), biochemical co-immunoprecipitation (C66-C69, C94, C117, C142-C148), and imaging studies (C63-C80, C160-C170). The claim that TIAM-1 functions independently of Rac1 GEF activity (C3) is supported by rescue with catalytically dead TIAM-1(T548F) mutants (C86-C89) and lack of phenotypes in rac mutants (C83-C84). The role of HPO-30 in DMA-1 trafficking is supported by imaging and time-lapse experiments (C70-C80, C149-C153).

results.result: Genetic screens identified recessive alleles of dma-1/LRR-TM, hpo-30/Claudin, tiam-1/GEF, and act-4/Actin that affect PVD dendrite patterning. Cell-specific rescue experiments demonstrate that these genes function cell-autonomously in PVD neurons. The act-4(dz222) missense allele (G151E) is identical to an allele identified in an independent screen, and expression of any actin (ACT-1 or ACT-4) in PVD is sufficient for dendrite patterning.
results.evaluation: The genetic screen results are well-documented with molecular characterization of alleles (C19-C24) and cell-specific rescue experiments (C22, C28-C29). The claim that any actin is sufficient (C32) is supported by rescue with ACT-1 (C29). The act-4(dz222) allele identification is confirmed by independent isolation (C24, C120). All alleles affect both PVD and FLP neurons (C30), supporting a conserved mechanism.

results.result: The intracellular domain of DMA-1/LRR-TM is required for formation of PVD higher order branches. Specifically, the PDZ-binding site at the extreme C-terminus of DMA-1 is important for formation of 4° branches but not 2° or 3° branches. Complete removal of dma-1 results in almost complete absence of 3° and 4° branches with additional effects on 2° branches.
results.evaluation: The structure-function analysis of DMA-1 is supported by rescue experiments with deletion constructs (C34-C35) and CRISPR-engineered ΔPDZ mutants (C37-C38). The differential requirement for the PDZ motif in 4° versus 2°/3° branching (C37-C40) is clearly demonstrated by quantitative morphometric analysis shown in Figure 1G-I. The phenotype of complete dma-1 loss (C33) is supported by published literature and data in Figure 1B,C.

results.result: Genetic epistasis analysis reveals that hpo-30/Claudin and tiam-1/GEF act in the Menorin pathway to pattern PVD dendritic arbors. dma-1/LRR-TM is epistatic to both hpo-30 and tiam-1, suggesting it is required for most functions during patterning of higher order branches. Double mutants between tiam-1 and other pathway components (mnr-1, lect-2, kpc-1, sax-7, hpo-30, act-4) are more severe than single mutants but indistinguishable from dma-1 mutants, suggesting parallel pathways. hpo-30 and tiam-1 may also serve independent functions.
results.evaluation: The epistasis analysis is comprehensive and well-controlled, with quantitative morphometric data for 2°, 3°, and 4° branches shown in Figure 2E-G. The claim that dma-1 is epistatic (C43-C44) is supported by statistical analysis showing double mutants are indistinguishable from dma-1 single mutants. The evidence for parallel pathways (C45-C46) is strong, with double mutants showing enhancement. The suggestion of independent functions (C51) is appropriately qualified as speculative based on the genetic data.

results.result: Loss of hpo-30/Claudin, tiam-1/GEF, or act-4/Actin suppresses the formation of baobab-like dendritic arbors induced by ectopic expression of mnr-1/Menorin in muscle. Protein localization of LECT-2 or SAX-7 reporters is not visibly affected in these mutants, suggesting these genes function genetically downstream of or in parallel to mnr-1/Menorin.
results.evaluation: The gain-of-function suppression experiments (C52-C53) provide strong evidence for pathway ordering, with quantitative data shown in Figure 3A-E. The observation that upstream ligand localization is unaffected (C54) supports the conclusion that these genes act downstream. This is a well-established genetic approach for pathway ordering, and the results are consistent with the epistasis analysis.

results.result: Overexpression of tiam-1/GEF results in increased branching in PVD dendrites, which is completely suppressed by mutation in act-4/Actin. The tiam-1(o/e); act-4 double mutant is statistically indistinguishable from the act-4 single mutant. Overexpression of tiam-1 in dma-1 null mutants significantly increases the number of branches. These results suggest TIAM-1/GEF functions downstream of or in parallel to DMA-1/LRR-TM and in a manner that depends on ACT-4/Actin.
results.evaluation: The overexpression and suppression experiments (C56-C60) provide strong evidence for the genetic pathway ordering. The quantitative data in Figure 3F-M show statistically significant effects with appropriate controls. The epistasis relationship between tiam-1 and act-4 (C57-C59) is clearly demonstrated. The ability of tiam-1 overexpression to partially bypass dma-1 loss (C60) supports the pathway model (C61).

results.result: DMA-1/LRR-TM and HPO-30/Claudin are predicted transmembrane proteins that colocalize in PVD dendrites. DMA-1::GFP and HPO-30::tagBFP puncta show significant but not complete colocalization in dendritic processes. Co-immunoprecipitation experiments demonstrate that DMA-1 and HPO-30 are part of the same biochemical complex, and this interaction is independent of the intracellular domain of DMA-1, suggesting interaction through transmembrane segments or extracellular domains.
results.evaluation: The colocalization data (C63-C65) is supported by imaging in Figure 4A-D. The biochemical interaction (C66-C67) is demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation in Figure 4F. The structure-function analysis showing ICD-independence (C68-C69) is supported by co-IP with deletion constructs in Figure 4G. The combination of imaging and biochemical evidence provides strong support for a physical interaction between these proteins.

results.result: HPO-30/Claudin regulates DMA-1/LRR-TM surface expression and trafficking. Overexpression of HPO-30 reduces DMA-1::GFP fluorescent intensity in dendrites, while loss of hpo-30 increases diffuse dendrite staining of DMA-1::GFP in 3° dendrites. Time-lapse imaging shows that loss of hpo-30 reduces the number of mobile DMA-1::GFP puncta while immobile puncta remain unchanged. These findings suggest HPO-30 negatively regulates DMA-1 surface membrane levels and serves a function in trafficking of DMA-1 vesicles.
results.evaluation: The imaging experiments (C70-C72) are quantified in Figure 4H-O with appropriate statistical analysis. The interpretation that diffuse staining represents surface membrane and punctate staining represents vesicular fraction (C73) is supported by published literature. The time-lapse experiments (C75-C77) provide direct evidence for a role in trafficking, with quantification in Figure 4R. The conclusions (C78-C80) are well-supported by the imaging data, though the exact mechanism remains to be determined.

results.result: TIAM-1/GEF can function independently of its Rac1 GEF enzymatic activity during PVD patterning. Mutations in mig-2/RhoG, ced-10/Rac1, or rac-2 do not result in obvious PVD phenotypes. Transgenic expression of TIAM-1(T548F), a point mutant devoid of measurable Rac1 GEF activity in vitro, fully rescues the tiam-1 mutant phenotype. CRISPR-engineered alleles harboring the T548F mutation appear phenotypically normal.
results.evaluation: This is a surprising and important finding. The lack of phenotypes in rac mutants (C83) is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-C. The rescue with TIAM-1(T548F) (C86) is shown in Figure 6B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D. The CRISPR-engineered alleles (C88) provide strong evidence that the T548F mutation does not impair TIAM-1 function in vivo (Figure 6C-D). The claim that this mutation abolishes Rac1 GEF activity in vitro (C87) is supported by published literature. The conclusion (C90) is appropriately qualified with a caveat about possible activity toward other GTPases.

results.result: The PDZ-mediated interaction between TIAM-1/GEF and DMA-1/LRR-TM is required for normal 4° dendrite formation. Removing the PDZ ligand motif of DMA-1 or the PDZ domain of TIAM-1 results in specific loss of 4° branching. Co-immunoprecipitation assays demonstrate direct interaction through the PDZ motif and domain. TIAM-1 overexpression results in excessive branching, suggesting dose-dependent function. A TIAM-1::GFP reporter fails to localize to 4° branches in DMA-1(ΔPDZ) animals.
results.evaluation: The genetic evidence (C91-C92) is supported by rescue experiments shown in Figure 5B-E. The biochemical interaction (C94) is demonstrated by co-IP in Figure 5F-H. The dose-dependence (C95-C96) is supported by overexpression data in Figure 3. The localization data (C99) from published literature provides additional support. The proposed model of PDZ-mediated recruitment (C97) is a reasonable inference from the combined genetic, biochemical, and localization data.

results.result: Transgenic expression of TIAM-1(GEF-only) lacking the PDZ domain can rescue 2° and 3° PVD branches but not 4° branches. DMA-1 lacking the cytoplasmic domain can rescue 2° and 3° branching number but not extension. DMA-1 colocalizes with HPO-30/Claudin and both proteins form a biochemical complex independent of the DMA-1 cytoplasmic domain. Double mutant analyses show hpo-30 with tiam-1 or sax-7 display enhanced phenotypes consistent with parallel pathways.
results.evaluation: The rescue experiments (C101-C102) demonstrate differential requirements for different branch orders, supported by data in Figure 5 and Figure 1. The colocalization and biochemical interaction (C104-C105) are supported by imaging (Figure 4C-D) and co-IP (Figure 4F-G). The genetic epistasis (C106) is supported by data in Figure 2. These results collectively support a model of parallel pathways downstream of DMA-1, though the exact molecular mechanisms remain to be fully elucidated.

results.result: F-actin plays an important role in PVD dendrite formation. F-actin is localized to the distal tips of developing PVD dendrites and appears mutually exclusive with microtubules. F-actin localization depends on transmembrane receptors and their ligands. The DMA-1/LRR-TM receptor is part of a biochemical complex with TIAM-1/GEF and ACT-4/Actin. A model is proposed where binding of DMA-1 by the SAX-7/MNR-1/LECT-2 ligand complex results in recruitment of TIAM-1/GEF and ACT-4/Actin, directly linking the receptor to the cytoskeleton.
results.evaluation: The localization of F-actin to distal dendrites (C114) is demonstrated by UtrCH reporter imaging in Figure 7A. The dependence on pathway components (C115) is shown in Figure 7B-C. The biochemical complex (C117) is demonstrated by co-IP in Figure 7D-F. The proposed molecular clutch model (C118) is a reasonable inference from the combined genetic, biochemical, and imaging data, though it remains speculative and requires further testing. The role of F-actin (C113) is supported by published literature showing depolymerization causes severe defects.

results.result: The interaction between TIAM-1/GEF and ACT-4/Actin is likely specific, as animals carrying the act-4(dz222) missense allele are viable without other obvious phenotypes. The G151E mutation was independently identified in another screen. Loss of ACT-4 by RNAi and the G151E missense mutation result in similar PVD phenotypes, suggesting the interaction between TIAM-1 and ACT-4 must be transient or dynamic. Alternatively, the strong interaction between ACT-4(G151E) and TIAM-1 could sequester actin from the polymerizing pool.
results.evaluation: The specificity of the act-4(dz222) allele (C119) is supported by the viable phenotype and independent isolation (C120). The comparison between RNAi and missense mutation (C121-C122) provides evidence that both loss and gain of interaction are detrimental. The inference about dynamic interaction (C124) is reasonable based on the phenotypic data (C123), though alternative explanations (C125) are appropriately considered. The analogy to β-spectrin (C126) from published literature provides supporting context.

results.result: TIAM-1 co-immunoprecipitates ACT-4 from cell lysates. The ACT-4 G151E missense mutation dramatically increases the strength of the biochemical interaction with TIAM-1. Deletion of individual domains of TIAM-1 fails to abrogate the interaction with ACT-4, suggesting multiple domains may bind ACT-4 in a partially redundant fashion. ACT-4 can be precipitated with DMA-1, with the interaction possibly stronger in the presence of TIAM-1. TIAM-1 is part of a complex containing both DMA-1 and ACT-4, potentially directly linking the receptor to the cytoskeleton.
results.evaluation: The co-IP experiments (C142-C143) are shown in Figure 7D-E with clear bands. The domain deletion analysis (C144) is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B. The three-way interaction (C147) is demonstrated in Figure 7F. The conclusion that TIAM-1 links DMA-1 to ACT-4 (C148) is well-supported by the biochemical data, though the stoichiometry and dynamics of the complex remain to be determined. The dramatic increase in binding with G151E (C143) provides a molecular explanation for the mutant phenotype.

results.result: Both membrane surface levels and trafficking of DMA-1/LRR-TM reporter are affected by the amount of HPO-30/Claudin expressed in PVD. Loss of hpo-30 increases membrane surface staining, while overexpression decreases it. Loss of hpo-30 also reduces the fraction of mobile vesicles containing DMA-1::GFP. These findings suggest HPO-30 promotes internalization and trafficking of DMA-1. This is consistent with a recent study showing HPO-30 negatively regulates NLG-1/Neuroligin at the cholinergic NMJ.
results.evaluation: The imaging experiments (C149-C152) are quantified in Figure 4H-R with appropriate statistical analysis. The conclusion about internalization and trafficking (C153) is a reasonable inference from the bidirectional effects of HPO-30 levels on DMA-1 localization. The consistency with published work on NLG-1 (C154) provides additional support for a general role of HPO-30 in regulating surface protein levels. The mechanism of regulation remains to be fully elucidated.

results.result: F-actin, visualized by tagRFP::UtrCH, localizes to defined subcellular compartments during PVD dendrite development. During L2 stage, UtrCH is localized to cell body and 1°, 2°, and budding 3° branches. In subsequent stages, it becomes more localized to distal developing branches. Microtubules, visualized by tagRFP::TBA-1, are primarily localized to axons and 1° dendrites. The mutually exclusive localization of F-actin and microtubules is lost in mutants of the Menorin pathway, with F-actin relocalizing to more proximal dendrites and microtubules found in more distal dendrites. These results suggest the Menorin pathway establishes polarity and functions to localize F-actin to growing dendrites.
results.evaluation: The developmental time course of F-actin localization (C160-C164) is clearly documented in Figure 7A. The microtubule localization (C165) is shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1 and consistent with published literature. The mutual exclusivity (C166) and its loss in mutants (C167-C169) are demonstrated in Figure 7B-C and Figure 7—figure supplement 1. The conclusion about polarity establishment (C170) is a reasonable inference from the imaging data, though the molecular mechanisms remain to be determined.

results.result: At least two partially redundant pathways act downstream of the DMA-1/LRR-TM receptor. In one pathway, DMA-1 interacts via HPO-30/Claudin with the WRC during patterning of lower order branches. In another pathway, the interaction with TIAM-1/GEF may directly link the receptor complex with the actin cytoskeleton during 4° dendrite formation.
results.evaluation: This is a synthesis claim that integrates findings from this study and published work (C127). The model of two pathways (C128-C129) is supported by the differential effects of PDZ deletion (affecting only 4° branches), the ability of GEF-only TIAM-1 to rescue 2°/3° but not 4° branches, the enhanced phenotypes in certain double mutants, and the published work on HPO-30/WRC interactions. While the model is well-supported by the genetic and biochemical data, some aspects remain speculative and require further validation.

results.result: Background and context claims about dendrite morphology in neurological disorders, the importance of F-actin and microtubules in neuronal development, the role of Tiam1 in vertebrates, the development of PVD dendritic arbors through successive orthogonal branching, and the Menorin/SAX-7/LECT-2/DMA-1 pathway in PVD patterning. The signaling mechanisms downstream of DMA-1 have remained largely elusive prior to this study.
results.evaluation: These claims (C7-C18) provide established background knowledge and context for the study. They are supported by appropriate citations to published literature (C7, C9, C10, C11, C14, C15, C16) or represent general knowledge in the field (C8, C12, C13). The statement about limited knowledge of downstream signaling (C18) accurately describes the state of the field prior to this work. These claims are well-supported but represent background rather than novel findings.

results.result: The G151E mutation in act-4 is analogous to a dominant allele in ACTA1 in a human patient with severe congenital myopathy. A reporter for act-4 is expressed in muscle, but fluorescence in situ hybridization experiments also suggested neuronal expression.
results.evaluation: The analogy to human ACTA1 (C25) is supported by published literature and provides important context for the mutation. The expression pattern claims (C26-C27) are supported by published literature and unpublished data. These claims provide important context for understanding the act-4 gene but are not primary findings of this study.

results.result: Previous studies have shown that mutating components of the WRC results in defects in PVD patterning. HPO-30 can physically interact with the WRC, and compromising interactions between DMA-1/TIAM-1 and HPO-30/WRC result in synergistic defects. Zou et al. proposed that DMA-1, HPO-30, and TIAM-1 recruit actin regulators to the membrane. Alternatively, recruitment of WRC by HPO-30 may serve a role in endocytosis of DMA-1. The act-4(dz222) allele results in more distal localization of DMA-1::GFP.
results.evaluation: These claims (C107-C112) primarily cite and discuss published work by Zou et al. (2018) and others. The observation about act-4(dz222) affecting DMA-1 localization (C112) is supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D,E. The alternative model about endocytosis (C111) is appropriately presented as speculative. These claims provide important context and discussion of related work but are not primary findings of this study.

results.result: Tiam1 in vertebrates serves important functions during nervous system patterning, including axon growth cone formation and activity-dependent dendrite remodeling. The Drosophila and C. elegans homologs function in synaptic and axonal patterning. All known functions of Tiam1 appear dependent on canonical GEF activity. The finding that TIAM-1 can function independently of Rac1 activity during PVD patterning is novel. There is only one other known example of GEF-independent function (DOCK7). GEF-independent functions that directly modulate the cytoskeleton may be an underappreciated property of GEFs.
results.evaluation: The background on Tiam1 functions (C130-C133) is well-supported by published literature. The evidence for GEF-independent function in this study (C134-C138) is strong, as discussed in the main result evaluation. The claim about DOCK7 (C139-C140) is supported by published literature. The speculation about underappreciated GEF-independent functions (C141) is a reasonable inference but remains to be tested more broadly. This represents important discussion and contextualization of the findings.

results.result: Several speculative explanations for the functional significance of DMA-1 regulation by HPO-30 are proposed: (1) surface expression may need tight regulation to avoid too strong binding to ligands, (2) recycling may be required for DMA-1 to remain functional, (3) recycling may be necessary for transport to locations of demand, and (4) internalization may be part of signal transduction itself.
results.evaluation: These claims (C155-C159) are explicitly speculative explanations for the observed regulation of DMA-1 by HPO-30. While the speculation is reasonable and supported by analogy to other systems (C157, C159 cite published literature), these are proposed models rather than tested hypotheses. The authors appropriately present these as possible explanations that require further investigation. No direct experimental evidence is provided to distinguish between these alternatives.
